name: Jamal Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Jamal, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. You can tell me the public version and the private version.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I'll probably surprise you, I'm the guy on site who loves the gadgets but goes to church on Sunday and votes for lower taxes. People don't know what box to put me in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Ha, no boxes here. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small firm out in the country, building barns, stables and timber farm sheds, so a lot of big posts, roof purlins and cladding. I'm the junior carpenter, three years in, because before that I drove a parcel van for twenty years until my knees and the delivery apps wore me down. I use AI every single day, I take a photo of the plan and get it to make my cutting list, and in the evenings I watch videos and ask it questions about joints I haven't done before. I love being out in the fields at sunrise with a barn going up. What wears me out is the travel, an hour each way down country lanes, because there's no work like this near town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, it's a tool, use it like any other tool. I'd keep telling the older guys on site to use it for their cutting lists, and they'd keep telling me to put my phone away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be fine for me, maybe even good. If everyone else gives up on AI and I keep using it, I'm faster than I should be for a three-year carpenter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with the firm, keep learning, and keep using AI for planning and quotes. I'd start taking small weekend jobs, garden offices and log stores, to build up my own customers. The long-term plan is my own small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty upbeat, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want to be doing in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running my own crew, building garden rooms and small barns. Me, a van, maybe two guys, and the computer doing the drawings and quotes. Nobody handing me anything, just my name on the side of the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How's money at home at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Lena works part-time in the church office doing the books, I'm on the junior rate, and the mortgage takes a big chunk. We've got maybe three weeks of money saved, and the van's my old courier van with two hundred thousand on the clock.

S0.say: Great, it's a tool, so use it like any other tool. I'd keep telling the older guys on site to use it for their cutting lists, and they'd keep telling me to put my phone away.
S0.think: It'd be fine for me, maybe even good. If everyone else gives up on AI and I keep using it, I'm faster than I should be for a three-year carpenter.
S0.do: Keeps working for the rural building firm and uses AI for planning and quotes. Starts taking small weekend jobs such as garden offices and log stores, working towards his own small firm.
S0.quote: Nobody handing me anything, just my name on the side of the van.
S0.fieldNote: He is a rare mix of keen tech user and traditional, free-market values. He sees AI as a way to make up for coming late to carpentry. Owning his own small firm is the ambition that shapes everything he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity, and the people who learn fastest will do best. I'd say government should keep out of the way and let small businesses get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do well. I'm already the one on site who uses the tech, so I'd become more useful, not less. I worry a bit about the older guys, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every new tool the firm brings in and teach myself the ones it doesn't. I'd grow the weekend jobs, use AI for drawings and quotes, and maybe rent a small machine for lifting posts if it saves me a man. The aim would be to go self-employed in two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Excited, honestly, like the first day on a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your own firm. How does that fit with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It fits perfectly. If machines and AI make it cheaper to do the drawings and the heavy lifting, a small guy like me can compete with the big firms. That's what I want, a fair chance to build something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for people to learn the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The person who wants the skill, mostly, and the firms if it helps them. I learned most of what I know from videos and my phone at the kitchen table after the kids are asleep. I don't think anyone owes me lessons.

S1.say: This is an opportunity, and the people who learn fastest will do best. Government should keep out of the way and let small businesses get on with it.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because I'm already the one on site who uses the tech. I'd become more useful, not less, though I worry a bit about the older guys.
S1.do: Learns every new tool his firm brings in and teaches himself the rest, while growing his weekend jobs with AI-made drawings and quotes. Considers renting a small post-lifting machine and aims to go self-employed within two or three years.
S1.feel: Excited, like the first day on a new job.
S1.quote: I learned most of what I know from videos and my phone at the kitchen table after the kids are asleep.
S1.fieldNote: He sees the steady picture as a way for small firms to compete with big ones, which matches his free-market views. He believes individuals should mostly pay for their own learning. His concern for older colleagues is real but brief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and people need to move fast. I'd still say government shouldn't take over, but they'd have to make sure families aren't left on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. If AI can do almost any job, including running a small firm, where's the opportunity? And I've got no savings to buy into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get in early with whoever is selling or renting the building robots, either working for them or using one for my weekend jobs. I'd do as many cash jobs as I could while people still want a person. And we'd cut back straight away at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd be busy, which helps. It's like getting sixty parcels at seven in the morning and knowing you have to get them all out by night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with the slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, there's no time to build a business slowly. In the slower picture, I'd grow the weekend jobs over years. With two years, I'd have to bet on something quick and hope it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd want your own firm. Could you afford to start one in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, not without a loan, and I hate debt. Maybe my brother-in-law could go in with me on a machine, or the church men who run businesses might help. But it'd be a gamble, and I'm gambling with Max and Hannah's dinners.

S2.say: This is huge, and people need to move fast. Government shouldn't take over, but it would have to make sure families aren't left on the street.
S2.think: It worries me, because if AI can do almost any job, including running a small firm, where's the opportunity? And I've got no savings to buy into it.
S2.do: Tries to get in early with companies selling or renting building robots, either working for them or using one for his weekend jobs. Takes as many cash jobs as he can and cuts household spending straight away.
S2.feel: Nervous but busy, like a van loaded with sixty parcels to get out by night.
S2.quote: But it'd be a gamble, and I'm gambling with Max and Hannah's dinners.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture shakes his belief that being quick creates opportunity, because AGI could run small firms too. He still reaches for action, trying to use the robots rather than fight them. His dislike of debt clashes with his need for money to buy in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance, so get moving. Learn the new tools, start your own thing, don't wait for someone else to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is good for me. I could build my own small firm, using AI and robots, and be the one who owns the tools instead of the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, learn everything I can about the building robots and how they work. Grow the weekend jobs and save towards a deposit on a machine. By year three, buy or lease a used one, and go self-employed with my own small crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It feels like a race I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Definitely. I could spend money on a machine that's out of date in a year. That's why I'd lease first, and talk to people who are already doing it before I commit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd bet on the wrong thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And I'd keep an eye on the old guys from my firm, maybe hire one of them. Pete has forty years of knowing what a barn should look like, and a machine can't tell you that yet.

S3.say: Five years is a real chance, so get moving. Learn the new tools, start your own thing and don't wait for someone else to fix it.
S3.think: Five years is good for me. I could build my own small firm with AI and robots, and be the one who owns the tools instead of the one replaced by them.
S3.do: Learns everything he can about building robots in the first year and saves towards a machine from weekend jobs. By year three leases a used machine and goes self-employed with a small crew, possibly hiring an older colleague.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more excited than scared, as if in a race he could win.
S3.quote: Pete has forty years of knowing what a barn should look like, and a machine can't tell you that yet.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him picture owning the tools instead of being replaced by them. He has a sensible plan to lease before buying, to avoid betting on the wrong machine. Hiring an older colleague shows that respect for experience sits alongside his love of new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone not to prepare. Families, churches and small businesses can handle this without big government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years feels great for me. I'd have time to build my firm properly, learn the machines and get the kids grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, keep working, learn the robots, grow the weekend jobs and save. Then start my own firm, using the machines for the heavy lifting and the AI for the paperwork. I'd make sure the kids learn useful skills too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It feels like something I can plan and build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd build slowly and properly. Get really good at the trade first, then the business side, then buy machines when they're cheaper and better. No rushing, no big debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Max and Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Max to learn a trade alongside the tech, because the people who know both will always have work. And Hannah, she's bossy in the best way, maybe she runs the business one day. Family firm, Schmidt and Kids.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone not to prepare. Families, churches and small businesses can handle this without big government.
S4.think: Ten years feels great for me. I'd have time to build my firm properly, learn the machines and get the kids grown.
S4.do: Keeps working, learns the robots, grows his weekend jobs and saves over the first few years. Then starts his own firm using machines for heavy lifting and AI for paperwork, and makes sure his children learn useful skills.
S4.feel: Calm and a little excited, as something he can plan and build.
S4.quote: And Hannah, she's bossy in the best way, maybe she runs the business one day. Family firm, Schmidt and Kids.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he can build slowly and avoid debt, which fits both his caution about money and his appetite for new technology. He imagines a family business carried on by his children. His plan depends on machines becoming cheaper over time, which he assumes but can't know.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything and no money to buy in. What would help is cheap loans or leasing for small tradespeople to get the machines, and apprenticeships so people can learn them. Not handouts, a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'll own the robots. If it's only the big firms, guys like me are finished. If small tradesmen can own them too, it could be the best thing that ever happened to us.

headlineQuote: If it's only the big firms, guys like me are finished. If small tradesmen can own them too, it could be the best thing that ever happened to us.
portrait: Jamal is a 43-year-old junior carpenter building barns and stables for a small rural firm, who came to the trade after twenty years driving a parcel van. A churchgoer who favours lower taxes, he also uses AI every day for cutting lists and quotes and dreams of running his own small firm. He is calm in the plateau and steady pictures, anxious in the two-year AGI picture because he has no money to buy into the new machines, and calmer again with five or ten years to build slowly and avoid debt. He wants small tradespeople to be able to own robots, not just big firms, and asks for a ladder rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to build a business and no money to buy into the new machines.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or leasing so small tradespeople can get the machines, and apprenticeships to learn them.
